newsitem.title: FINLAND: Pulp prices depressed - Finnish forestry industry.
newsitem.headline: Pulp prices depressed - Finnish forestry industry.

text.p: Pulp prices have not risen according to plan due to higher inventories and increased pulp output in Asia, the Federation of Finnish Forest Industries said in a report on Wednesday.
Pulp prices are a leading price indicator for the paper sector and particularly for fine papers.
The federation said in its report that softwood pulp prices have been hovering at about $560 to $580 per tonne for about half a year, after rising from a trough of $480 per tonne.

"Even though the markets as such are growing very fast (in the Far East), the capacities come in very high steps, so occasionally we might see disturbances in America and Europe as well," the federation's new chairman Juha Niemela told a news conference at the federation's autumn meeting.
Niemela is also chief executive at UPM-Kymmene, Europe's biggest forest industry group.
Niemela said that if pulp prices remained at their current depressed level, only the most efficient producers would survive in the long term.
The federation said that North American and Scandinavian (Norscan) pulp inventories had risen again since the summer months and that this had dampened hopes for price rises.
Niemela told the news conference that with Norscan pulp inventories 200,000-300,000 tonnes above their equilibrium level of about 1.5 million tonnes, pulp prices remain unpredictable.
"It seems to be the kind of prickly situation from which pulp prices could in fact shoot in any direction whatsoever," he said.
Niemela also told the news conference that mill stoppages would be needed but that it was unclear whether the curtailments due at the end of the year would be enough.

"It is undeniable that Far Eastern pulp, and above all Indonesian production, has a clear impact on world prices. Staring exclusively at these so-called Norscan inventories is self-deception nowadays," Niemela added.
